hero.headline: Martin County opens $167 million in state funding for mobile home storm repairs after tornado tragedy
hero.body:
Nearly 140 new Florida laws took effect on July 1, and one of them could significantly help vulnerable homeowners across the state. Senate Bill 594 makes $167 million in state affordable housing funding available to mobile and manufactured home owners for emergency repairs and storm-hardening improvements. The law addresses a critical housing safety issue that affects hundreds of thousands of Floridians living in older homes that cannot withstand modern storms.

The push for this legislation came after an EF-3 tornado devastated the Spanish Lakes Country Club Community in Fort Pierce, destroying 138 homes and killing six residents. An investigation following the disaster revealed that nearly 700,000 manufactured homes across Florida, roughly two-thirds of the state's total, were built before current federal safety standards and are vulnerable to severe weather. Many residents, including Paula Richards from Spanish Lakes, cannot afford the estimated $10,000 to $15,000 needed for storm-hardening work. Lawmakers responded by passing Senate Bill 594 in spring 2026, expanding access to SHIP funding specifically for manufactured home emergency repairs and storm-hardening retrofits.

In Martin County, the application process will launch in August through an online portal. Julie Stellatos with Martin County Human Services explains that about 75 percent of the county's annual SHIP funding, typically between $1 million and $1.5 million, can now assist eligible mobile and manufactured homeowners. Applicants can either complete an online application or call the office to request a paper form. Stellatos notes that people were seeking assistance long before the law passed, and this funding represents a major opportunity. Across the viewing area, other counties are at different stages of implementation. Okeechobee County is updating its local housing assistance plan to comply with the law. St. Lucie County is still awaiting final state guidance before announcing its application process. Indian River County plans to present the matter to its board on August 18, with a September 30 deadline to submit its plan to the state.

Because funding is allocated on a first-come, first-served basis, Stellatos recommends that interested homeowners begin gathering necessary paperwork immediately. Applicants can visit the Florida Housing Finance Corporation website, select their county, and check income eligibility requirements while preparing their applications. The website also provides contact information and application instructions. As Paula Richards said following the tragedy, "Mobile home lives matter too." This new funding represents a concrete response to the needs of Florida's most vulnerable residents living in manufactured homes.

cards.headline: Palm Beach County residents face thousands in retroactive sewer fees from Delray Beach
cards.body:
Homeowners in an unincorporated Palm Beach County neighborhood are dealing with unexpected bills for unpaid sewer fees spanning several years, with some residents facing charges exceeding $4,000. The situation has left residents concerned about potential service disconnection if they cannot pay the amounts demanded by the city of Delray Beach.

Residents along Franwood Drive received notices demanding back payments following a city audit completed in April 2026. The bills include charges for up to three years of sewer service along with new monthly fees going forward. Candace Etzler received a notice for $3,139, and she reported that at least a dozen other homeowners in the neighborhood received similar notices. Her neighbor, Ruth Stephens, was billed $4,494.92. The retroactive billing stems from 1998, when nearby development disrupted the residents' septic systems. State law required them to connect to the closest municipal sewer system as a result. Stephens said residents had previously attempted to pay for sewer service but were told they did not need to do so.

Residents are challenging how the city calculated the back charges. Etzler questioned the methodology behind the 36-month calculation period and the $90 monthly rate the city applied. Stephens expressed frustration about the total amount, saying "I understand having to pay a monthly fee, but my total was $4,494.92, and that's hard for people to just come up with." Some residents have already paid the fees or signed up for payment plans out of concern that they could lose sewer service.

City Commissioner Juli Casale defended the billing approach in a written statement, explaining that when a sewer connection is identified, the city must determine accumulated costs and recover applicable fees from those using the service. She emphasized that the city is ensuring utility costs are paid by those receiving service rather than shifting expenses to other taxpayers. Meanwhile, County Commissioner Marci Woodward indicated she has been communicating with the county attorney's office regarding the legality of both the retroactive charges and the monthly payments being demanded from residents.

cards.headline: Florida moves to designate CAIR, Muslim Brotherhood, Antifa as terrorist organizations under new state law
cards.teaser: Governor Ron DeSantis announced Wednesday that Florida will designate several groups as terrorist organizations under a new state law that took effect July 1, m.
cards.body:
Governor Ron DeSantis announced Wednesday that Florida will immediately use a new state law to designate several groups as terrorist organizations. At a Tampa press conference with FDLE Commissioner Mark Glass and Statewide Prosecutor Brad McVay, DeSantis said the state is preparing its first designations under HB 1471, which took effect July 1. The list includes the Muslim Brotherhood, the Council on American-Islamic Relations (CAIR), Antifa, cartel-linked groups including Tren de Aragua and Sinaloa-related organizations, and Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. HB 1471, formally titled "Systems of Law and Terrorist Organizations," authorizes Florida's Chief of Domestic Security to recommend terrorist designations that must be approved or rejected by the governor and Florida Cabinet by majority vote. Designated organizations face public-funding restrictions, possible corporate dissolution in certain circumstances, and penalties tied to material support.

DeSantis framed the announcement as strengthening a December executive order targeting CAIR and the Muslim Brotherhood that was temporarily blocked by a judge in March after civil rights groups sued, arguing it violated constitutional protections. DeSantis said the new law provides better legal footing. The consequences could affect state and local funding, colleges and universities, and Florida's K-12 school-choice scholarship program. Following the announcement, attorneys representing CAIR said they expect another court fight. While the designations are not final until the Cabinet approves them, DeSantis said officials may meet in an emergency session to approve them despite no regular Cabinet meeting scheduled in July.

cards.headline: Downtown West Palm Beach road closures begin Thursday for 4th on Flagler celebration
cards.teaser: Several roads in downtown West Palm Beach will close starting Thursday afternoon ahead of the annual 4th on Flagler celebration. Closures will remain in effect through Sunday, July 5.
cards.body:
Drivers in downtown West Palm Beach should prepare for road closures beginning Thursday afternoon ahead of the annual 4th on Flagler celebration. Starting at 4 p.m. Thursday, July 2, several roads in the downtown area will close and remain closed through Sunday, July 5, according to the City of West Palm Beach.

The following road closures will be in effect: South Flagler Drive from Banyan Boulevard to Lakeview Avenue, the 100 blocks of Clematis Street, Datura Street and Evernia Street, the 200 blocks of Fern Street and Tanglewood Court, the 100 and 200 blocks of Trinity Place, Chase Avenue from Lakeview Avenue to South Flagler Drive, and Narcissus Avenue from Fern Street to Evernia Street. Drivers are encouraged to plan ahead, allow extra travel time and use alternate routes while the closures are in place. The annual 4th on Flagler celebration features live entertainment, family activities, food vendors and a fireworks display along the downtown waterfront.

cards.headline: Martin County manufactured home owners can apply for state repair funding starting in August
cards.teaser: Martin County manufactured home owners will be able to apply for state emergency repair and storm-hardening funding through an online portal opening in August, after a new law took effect Wednesday.
cards.body:
Nearly 140 new Florida laws took effect Wednesday, including Senate Bill 594, which opens up $167 million in state affordable housing funding to help mobile and manufactured home owners pay for emergency repairs and storm-hardening retrofits. The change follows an investigation that exposed hundreds of thousands of older homes across Florida that cannot stand up to today's storms. It started with an EF-3 tornado that obliterated manufactured homes in the Spanish Lakes Country Club Community of Fort Pierce, where 138 homes were lost and six residents were killed. The investigation found nearly 700,000 of Florida's more than 1 million mobile and manufactured homes were built before today's federal safety standards.

Julie Stellatos with Martin County Human Services says an online portal will open in August. Once it does, about 75 percent of the county's annual SHIP funding, typically $1 million to $1.5 million, could now help eligible mobile and manufactured homeowners. People can either fill out an online application or call the office and have one mailed to them. Okeechobee County officials said they are updating the county's local housing assistance plan to comply with the new law. St. Lucie County is still waiting on final guidance from the state before announcing its application process. Indian River County officials are taking the matter to the Board on August 18, with a deadline to submit their plan to the state by September 30. Stellatos said the funding is first come, first served.

cards.headline: North Palm Beach celebrates Fourth of July with fireworks and America 250 events at country club
cards.teaser: North Palm Beach Country Club and The Clubhouse will host a full day of Independence Day activities on July 4, including a pool party, live music and a 9 p.m. fireworks finale.
cards.body:
North Palm Beach will host a full day of Independence Day celebrations on July 4 at the North Palm Beach Country Club and The Clubhouse. The free community event combines family-friendly activities, live entertainment and fireworks to mark both the nation's birthday and America's 250th anniversary. According to event organizers, recognizing the milestone adds special significance to this year's annual holiday tradition in Palm Beach County.

The day begins at 11 a.m. with a community pool party at the country club pool area. Attendees can enjoy a water slide, DJ entertainment, games, activities, food and beverages, and a poolside satellite bar. Event organizers note that the pool deck and lawn areas will create a festive backdrop throughout the day. As the afternoon progresses, families can participate in lawn games and activities starting at 4:30 p.m., including cornhole, Connect 4, giant Jenga and face painting.

The Clubhouse will host a Fourth of July barbecue buffet beginning at 4:30 p.m., providing dinner options for guests. Live music from the band Solstice Reign is scheduled to begin around 6 p.m., adding entertainment to the evening festivities. Ashley Shipman, director of parks and recreation, highlighted that the golf course offers one of the best vantage points for viewing the fireworks display.

The celebration concludes with a fireworks finale at 9 p.m. The combination of activities, dining and entertainment makes the event accessible to visitors of all ages. With no admission fee and multiple entertainment options spread throughout the day, North Palm Beach's Fourth of July celebration provides a traditional way for residents and visitors to mark the holiday while also commemorating the country's 250-year milestone.

cards.headline: Meta complies with Florida youth social media law while TikTok, Google face enforcement action
cards.teaser: Attorney General James Uthmeier said Meta has suspended hundreds of thousands of underage accounts and is complying with Florida's social media law, but TikTok and Google have stayed silent on their compliance plans.
cards.body:
Florida's landmark social media law took effect after a major legal victory in November when the 11th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals cleared the way for implementation. HB 3, which bans children under 14 from creating social media accounts and requires parental consent for users ages 14 and 15, passed the Legislature in March 2024 and was signed that same month by Governor Ron DeSantis. The law represented a signature priority for then-House Speaker Paul Renner, who argued that "a child in their brain development doesn't have the ability to know that they're being sucked into these addictive technologies."

Attorney General James Uthmeier moved swiftly to enforce the law after defeating Big Tech's legal challenge. He warned noncompliant platforms of $50,000-per-violation fines that could accumulate into billions of dollars. Meta responded by announcing compliance effective in early May, and Uthmeier confirmed that Meta has suspended hundreds of thousands of accounts belonging to underage users. By contrast, TikTok and Google, which owns YouTube and YouTube Kids, have remained silent about their compliance plans and have effectively ignored the law's requirements.

Uthmeier sued TikTok in June for violating HB 3 by allowing underage accounts to persist and failing to secure parental consent from older teens. "TikTok knowingly deceives parents and allows children to be exposed to harmful and inappropriate content in direct violation of Florida law," Uthmeier stated. He emphasized that "we have zero tolerance for companies that prioritize profit over children's safety." At a subsequent press conference, Uthmeier directed his message toward other holdouts, telling YouTube and other platforms: "You got to wake up. This is real and you can save lives."

Google's continued silence is particularly striking given YouTube's dominance in teens' online activities. Research from Pew found that roughly 90 percent of U.S. teenagers use YouTube, surpassing all other platforms, with about 75 percent using it daily. The exposure risks are well documented: 46 percent of parents with children ages 11 and younger who use YouTube reported their child had encountered inappropriate content on the platform. Even YouTube Kids, which is rated for ages 4 and up, has been found to serve children content on topics like gender ideology and systemic racism, according to congressional testimony. Whether Google, TikTok, Roblox, and other platforms will follow Meta's lead remains uncertain. If they do not comply, Uthmeier indicated that companies "will have to open up your checkbook."

cards.headline: West Palm Beach gets $2 million state funding for Australian Avenue flood repairs
cards.teaser: Storm-weary drivers and residents along Australian Avenue in West Palm Beach could finally see relief after years of flooding. The new Florida budget includes $2 million in state funding for a long-discussed drainage project along the corridor.
cards.body:
The new Florida budget signed Monday by Gov. Ron DeSantis includes $2 million in state funding for a drainage project along Australian Avenue, a roadway neighbors say has flooded for as long as they can remember. The project targets Australian Avenue from Banyan Boulevard through 45th Street, an area Palm Beach County leaders have identified as needing major drainage improvements. Residents said even routine rain can leave streets underwater. Theodore Vanriel, who lives near the corridor, told WPTV that flooding has affected his daily commute to work since childhood, including times when he rode his bike through flooded streets during light storms.

State Sen. Mack Bernard said securing funding for the project was a major step forward after previous setbacks. Gov. Ron DeSantis vetoed $742,000 for the project last June. The $2 million in funding covers only a portion of the project's estimated $65 million cost. Palm Beach County Public Works Director and Engineer David Ricks presented plans three years ago that included creating a larger median and expanding road and shoulder areas to make room for larger underground drainage pipes designed to reduce flooding. According to Palm Beach County documents, the Australian Avenue improvements are part of a five-year road program scheduled to run through 2029.

cards.headline: Palm Beach International Airport transitions to Donald J. Trump International Airport
cards.teaser: Palm Beach International Airport is in the process of becoming Donald J. Trump International Airport, with the official name change set to take effect July 9. Signs are already being swapped out as part of a transition funded by the state of Florida at a cost of $2.75 million.
cards.body:
Palm Beach International Airport officially becomes Donald J. Trump International Airport on July 9, with the three-letter airport designation changing from PBI to DJT in August. The designation is used for airline reservations and navigation purposes. The airport remains owned by Palm Beach County, though Trump owns the trademark on the new name. Sign changes are being funded by the state of Florida at a cost of $2.75 million and will happen gradually, with passengers likely noticing the transition as it unfolds.

Airport officials said nothing should change for passengers beyond the signage. The airport posted a statement on its website saying: "While we recognize that the required name change may be received in different ways by our passengers, we're grateful for your continued support through this transition period." Two lawsuits are attempting to stop the name change. Local pilot George Poncy, one of the plaintiffs suing to block it, said the state appears to be stalling and delaying any hearing before a judge, noting it's possible the hearing could be scheduled after the name change takes effect.

cards.headline: Martin County clinic adds capacity after ACA subsidies expire, leaving residents without insurance
cards.teaser: Volunteers in Medicine in Martin County is seeing more patients after enhanced subsidies through the Affordable Care Act expired at the start of this year. The clinic says it has room for more people who need help.
cards.body:
Volunteers in Medicine, a free clinic serving low-income families in Martin County, is experiencing increased patient visits after enhanced Affordable Care Act subsidies expired at the start of 2024. The expiration of the enhanced financial assistance program has left many people without health insurance and, in some cases, without access to medical care. Dr. Jordan Bromberg, medical director of Volunteers in Medicine, said the loss of coverage affected more than 200,000 people in Florida who did not renew their health insurance through the ACA this year. "There are a lot of things that get screened for that if they're found early can prevent terrible outcomes," Bromberg said.

So far, only about 20 patients have turned to the clinic after losing ACA coverage, but estimates show there could be upwards of 500 people in Martin County who lost access. Bromberg said the clinic has capacity to serve more patients. To qualify for care at Volunteers in Medicine, individuals must earn under $39,990 per year, or under $82,500 for a family of four. The clinic provides free medical care with no strings attached. Patient Rokaya McGarry said she could no longer afford health insurance after the enhanced ACA subsidies expired and called the clinic when she became very ill. "I can't even express how grateful I am to them because I don't know where I'd be," McGarry said.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce tornado survivor questions how to access new Florida mobile home repair funding
cards.teaser: Senate Bill 594 opens up $167 million in state affordable housing funding to help mobile and manufactured home owners pay for emergency repairs and storm-hardening retrofits. The law took effect Wednesday.
cards.body:
An EF-3 tornado that obliterated manufactured homes in the Spanish Lakes Country Club Community of Fort Pierce killed six residents and destroyed 138 homes. Spanish Lakes resident Paula Richards received multiple repair estimates ranging from $10,000 to $15,000, costs she cannot afford. The tornado prompted an investigation that found nearly 700,000 of Florida's more than 1 million mobile and manufactured homes were built before current federal safety standards, leaving them unable to withstand modern storms.

Senate Bill 594 took effect July 1st, expanding access to $167 million in state SHIP funding for mobile and manufactured home owners to pay for lot rent, emergency repairs and storm-hardening retrofits. Julie Stellatos with Martin County Human Services said an online portal will open in August, allowing about 75 percent of the county's annual SHIP funding, typically $1 million to $1.5 million, to help eligible mobile and manufactured homeowners. Okeechobee County officials said they are updating the county's local housing assistance plan to comply with the new law and plan to offer lot rent, rehabilitation and emergency repair assistance for manufactured home owners once the program opens. St. Lucie County said it is still waiting on final guidance from the state before announcing its application process.

cards.headline: Jensen Beach teen Harper Aberman to represent Team USA at Sailing World Championship in France
cards.teaser: Harper Aberman of Jensen Beach is set to represent Team USA at the Sailing World Championship in France this weekend. Racing is set to begin Monday.
cards.body:
Harper Aberman, a Jensen Beach teenager, will represent Team USA at the Sailing World Championship in France this weekend. Her competitive sailing career began at age four when her grandparents enrolled her in a four-week summer camp in Pennsylvania. After attending for eight weeks, Aberman joined the green fleet program at the US Sailing Center of Martin County when her family moved to Jensen Beach, where she says her sailing adventure took off.

Aberman has won countless tournaments and placed in several national competitions, establishing herself as one of the biggest names in the youth sailing circuit. She describes herself as an adrenaline junkie drawn to the sport's most challenging conditions. She learned of her Team USA selection during Spring Break via email. Aberman has spent the past few weeks training in Spain ahead of the competition, with racing set to begin Monday.

cards.headline: West Palm Beach woman raises funds for best friend's family after Venezuela earthquakes kill relatives
cards.teaser: Alessandra De La Correa lost her grandmother, uncle, his wife, and 17-year-old cousin after two devastating earthquakes struck Venezuela's coastal city of La Guaira last week.
cards.body:
Alessandra De La Correa spent six agonizing hours wondering whether her parents were alive after two devastating earthquakes struck Venezuela's coastal city of La Guaira last week, collapsing buildings and killing several family members. Her best friend since high school, Carla Alvarado, who now lives in West Palm Beach, woke De La Correa with nonstop phone calls in the middle of the night. De La Correa's parents survived, but she lost her 17-year-old cousin Claudia, her grandmother, her uncle and his wife. Claudia, who had planned to study dentistry, was rehearsing a dance routine with classmates when the building collapsed. The earthquakes also destroyed her parents' home and businesses, including her mother's children's clothing store located in a shopping mall that collapsed entirely.

The losses came just weeks after De La Correa returned from her first visit to Venezuela in several years, where she announced she and her partner are expecting a baby later this year. Feeling powerless from abroad, Alvarado launched a GoFundMe campaign aiming to raise $15,000 to support De La Correa's relatives. De La Correa said the support from friends and strangers has become a lifeline as her parents return daily to the ruins of their apartment building searching for salvageable belongings. They managed to recover some clothing, photos and documents, but her uncle couldn't recover even one fork from his apartment.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce man arrested on drug trafficking charges after meth, MDMA seized
cards.teaser: A Fort Pierce man faces drug trafficking charges after deputies found methamphetamine and MDMA during a search.
cards.body:
A Fort Pierce man was arrested after deputies found drugs during a search on Wednesday, according to law enforcement. The search led to the discovery of methamphetamine and MDMA. The man now faces drug trafficking charges related to the seized narcotics.

Deputies conducted the search that resulted in the arrest. The investigation remains active as authorities process the evidence collected during the operation.

cards.headline: Man arrested after driving truck into Indian River County convenience store
cards.teaser: A driver was arrested after crashing a truck into a convenience store in Indian River County on Wednesday.
cards.body:
A man was arrested after driving a truck into a convenience store in Indian River County on Wednesday. The crash occurred at a local convenience store, causing property damage. Law enforcement responded to the scene and arrested the driver.

Authorities have not released details about what led to the crash or whether anyone was injured. The driver was taken into custody following the incident.

cards.headline: Dave & Buster's employee in Port St. Lucie stops suspected impaired driver
cards.teaser: A Port St. Lucie Dave & Buster's employee was praised for stopping a suspected impaired driver.
cards.body:
A Dave & Buster's employee in Port St. Lucie was hailed for stopping a suspected impaired driver. The employee took action when they observed signs of impairment, preventing the individual from driving. Law enforcement was contacted and responded to the scene.

The employee's intervention was recognized as potentially preventing a dangerous situation on local roads. Police handled the driver according to standard procedures for suspected impaired driving cases.

cards.headline: St. Lucie scanner Facebook page distances itself from founder after Orbeez arrest
cards.teaser: A St. Lucie County Facebook page that monitors law enforcement activity has distanced itself from its founder following an arrest involving Orbeez.
cards.body:
A St. Lucie County Facebook page that tracks law enforcement scanner activity has distanced itself from its founder after the individual was arrested in connection with an Orbeez incident. The page, which provides updates on police and fire activity in the area, announced it was separating from its creator following the arrest.

The Facebook page is popular among local residents who follow police and emergency response activity in St. Lucie County. The administrators took steps to publicly separate the page's operations from the founder after the arrest was made public.

Aberman has spent the past few weeks training in Spain ahead of the competition. Racing is set to begin Monday, with Aberman describing the preparation as involving a lot of recovery and time on the water.

Residents say the roadway has flooded for as long as they can remember, even during light rain. Theodore Vanriel, who lives near the corridor, has been riding his bike through flooded streets since he was a child. Marion Hawkins, another resident nearby, calls it "Lake Australian Avenue" and described water pushing into driveways and leaving debris scattered across properties after storms.

The $2 million covers only a portion of the project's estimated $65 million cost. Palm Beach County Public Works Director and Engineer David Ricks presented plans for improvements three years ago that included creating a larger median and expanding road and shoulder areas to make room for larger underground drainage pipes designed to reduce flooding. According to Palm Beach County documents, the Australian Avenue improvements are part of a five-year road program scheduled to run through 2029.

cards.headline: Benjamin Franklin artifact collection to open at Historical Society of Palm Beach County next week
cards.teaser: One of the largest collections of Benjamin Franklin artifacts will go on display at the Historical Society of Palm Beach County in downtown West Palm Beach starting next week.
cards.body:
One of the largest collections of Benjamin Franklin artifacts will open at the Historical Society of Palm Beach County next week. Zachary Jacobson of Palm Beach Gardens owns the collection with his brother, and they are displaying it to celebrate America's 250th birthday. The exhibit, titled Benjamin Franklin: Creating an American Icon, features over 50 books written by, printed by or about Franklin, along with work from his time as a printer. Artwork of the founding father covers the walls, including an original portrait. Among the standout pieces is a grandfather clock originally from Franklin's home in Philadelphia, a plate inscribed "B. Franklin," and original medallions made when Franklin was representing France during the American Revolution.

Jacobson's stepfather started the collection 50 years ago. Jacobson and his brother eventually bought the remains of the collection and continued it for 15 years. More than 120 pieces are on display. The exhibit covers the full scope of who Franklin was as a statesman, printer and inventor, including the glass armonica, which Franklin called his favorite invention. The exhibition also includes a copy of Experiments and Observations on Electricity Made at Philadelphia, owned by Franklin's son William, and a plaster model for the Libertas Americana medal. The free exhibit opens July 6 and runs through August at the Historical Society of Palm Beach County, located at 300 N Dixie Hwy.

cards.headline: Martin County free clinic sees more patients after ACA subsidies expired, has room for more
cards.teaser: Volunteers in Medicine in Martin County is seeing more patients after enhanced subsidies through the Affordable Care Act expired at the start of this year.
cards.body:
Volunteers in Medicine, a free clinic serving low-income families in Martin County, is seeing an increase in patients after enhanced subsidies through the Affordable Care Act expired at the start of this year. Dr. Jordan Bromberg, medical director of the clinic, said more than 200,000 people in Florida did not renew their health insurance through the ACA this year. While only about 20 patients have turned to the clinic after losing ACA coverage, estimates show there could be upwards of 500 people in Martin County who lost access to health insurance. Bromberg said the clinic has capacity to serve more patients.

Rokaya McGarry is among those who sought care at Volunteers in Medicine after the enhanced ACA subsidies expired and she could no longer afford health insurance. She said she began to see medical care as a luxury until she fell very ill after losing her mother. She called the clinic and within a day they provided care. To qualify for care at Volunteers in Medicine, individuals must earn under $39,990 per year, or under $82,500 for a family of four.

cards.headline: Alligator Alcatraz detention facility closed after one year of controversy
cards.teaser: One year after Florida opened Alligator Alcatraz, the controversial immigration detention facility in the Everglades has closed, leaving questions about its $1 billion cost.
cards.body:
President Donald Trump announced the opening of Alligator Alcatraz alongside Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis on July 1, 2025. The state used emergency powers to commandeer an old landing strip belonging to Miami-Dade County, then used emergency funding and no-bid contracts through the Florida Division of Emergency Management to build the facility in eight days. Trump said FEMA would pay for the facility, but a $608 million FEMA grant approved in October was stalled, leaving Florida taxpayers to cover the costs. Most estimates put the total price tag at more than $1 billion. The facility immediately faced criticism, with immigration attorneys raising alarms about conditions inside and the American Civil Liberties Union filing a federal lawsuit over detainees' access to legal counsel.

ICE confirmed on June 16 that all detainees had been removed in preparation for hurricane season. DeSantis said 21,000 detainees were deported through Alligator Alcatraz during its operation. Friends of the Everglades Director Eve Samples joined forces with the Miccosukee Tribe and other environmental groups to file a federal lawsuit claiming the construction violated the National Environmental Policy Act. The ACLU and Friends of the Everglades lawsuits remain active.

hero.headline: Jensen Beach teen Harper Aberman to represent Team USA at Sailing World Championship in France
hero.body:
A Jensen Beach teenager will represent Team USA at the Sailing World Championship in France this weekend, following years of competitive sailing that started at age four. Harper Aberman's journey into the sport began when her grandparents enrolled her in a four-week summer camp in Pennsylvania. While her cousin disliked the experience, Aberman was immediately drawn to sailing and chose to extend her stay to eight weeks.

After her family relocated to Jensen Beach, Aberman joined the green fleet program at the US Sailing Center of Martin County, where her competitive sailing career truly took off. She describes herself as an adrenaline junkie and is particularly attracted to challenging conditions on the water. "When it's windy, I've always struggled to stay upright and stay out of the water," Aberman said, acknowledging the difficulty of sailing in rough seas.

Despite downplaying her own abilities, Aberman has achieved significant success in youth sailing. She has won numerous tournaments, placed in several national competitions, and has become recognized as one of the biggest names in the youth sailing circuit. Learning that she would represent Team USA came as a surprise during Spring Break. "It was during Spring Break, I got the email. I started screaming, my parents started screaming, and we were like, 'This is not real. We're going to Europe this summer,'" Aberman said.

In preparation for the championship, Aberman has spent recent weeks training in Spain ahead of the Monday start of racing. She emphasized the importance of recovery and dedication leading up to the competition. "We plan on taking the waters Monday for racing, and it's just been a lot of recovery and a lot of time and effort out on the water, but it's definitely going to be worth it. Especially in the venue we're in," Aberman said. The combination of her early introduction to sailing, competitive achievements, and rigorous training has positioned her well for representing her country on the international stage.

cards.headline: Martin County manufactured home owners can apply for state repair funding starting in August
cards.teaser: Martin County manufactured home owners will be able to apply for state emergency repair and storm-hardening funding through an online portal opening in August, after a new law took effect Wednesday.
cards.body:
Nearly 140 new Florida laws took effect Wednesday, including Senate Bill 594, which opens up $167 million in state affordable housing funding to help mobile and manufactured home owners pay for emergency repairs and storm-hardening retrofits. The change follows an investigation that exposed hundreds of thousands of older homes across Florida that cannot stand up to today's storms. It started with an EF-3 tornado that obliterated manufactured homes in the Spanish Lakes Country Club Community of Fort Pierce, where 138 homes were lost and six residents were killed. The investigation found nearly 700,000 of Florida's more than 1 million mobile and manufactured homes were built before today's federal safety standards.

Julie Stellatos with Martin County Human Services says an online portal will open in August. Once it does, about 75 percent of the county's annual SHIP funding, typically $1 million to $1.5 million, could now help eligible mobile and manufactured homeowners. People can either fill out an online application or call the office and have one mailed to them. Okeechobee County officials said they are updating the county's local housing assistance plan to comply with the new law. St. Lucie County is still waiting on final guidance from the state before announcing its application process. Indian River County officials are taking the matter to the Board on August 18, with a deadline to submit their plan to the state by September 30. Stellatos said the funding is first come, first served.

cards.headline: Volunteers in Medicine clinic in Martin County sees more patients after ACA subsidies expired
cards.teaser: A free medical clinic in Martin County is seeing more patients after enhanced subsidies through the Affordable Care Act expired at the start of this year, and officials say the clinic has capacity for more.
cards.body:
Volunteers in Medicine, a free medical clinic in Martin County serving low-income families, is experiencing increased patient visits following the expiration of enhanced Affordable Care Act subsidies at the start of 2024. The clinic says the loss of financial assistance has left many people without health insurance and, in some cases, without access to medical care.

Dr. Jordan Bromberg, medical director of Volunteers in Medicine, noted that more than 200,000 people in Florida did not renew their health insurance through the ACA this year. While only about 20 patients have turned to the clinic after losing ACA coverage, estimates indicate there could be upwards of 500 people in Martin County who lost access to insurance. Bromberg said the clinic has capacity to serve more patients. The clinic provides free medical care with no strings attached. To qualify, individuals must earn under $39,990 per year, or under $82,500 for a family of four. Patient Rokaya McGarry said she could no longer afford health insurance after the subsidies expired and fell very ill following her mother's death. She called the clinic and within a day, Volunteers in Medicine took over her care.

cards.headline: Vero Beach nonprofit needs box truck to deliver 100 boxes of Venezuela earthquake relief supplies to Miami
cards.teaser: Latinas Nexus Network in Vero Beach has collected more than 100 boxes of supplies for Venezuela earthquake relief and is urgently calling on the community to donate the use of a box truck.
cards.body:
Latinas Nexus Network, a Vero Beach nonprofit, has collected more than 100 boxes of supplies for Venezuela earthquake relief and is partnering with Global Empowerment Mission in Miami to deliver them. The organization began collecting donations Friday afternoon in response to a 7.5-magnitude earthquake that struck Venezuela. Co-founder Juliana Marino said the community response exceeded expectations, with residents bringing donations of diapers, medical supplies, and other essentials. "The community has come together. They all came forward and brought something," Marino said.

However, the volume of donations has outpaced the organization's transportation capacity. The group initially planned to transport the boxes in personal vehicles to Miami, but ran out of space. Latinas Nexus Network is urgently seeking a box truck between 12 and 16 feet to move the supplies. Organizers need the truck no later than Thursday to load and deliver the supplies to Global Empowerment Mission on Friday. The effort is personal for founder Lourana Navarro, who was born in Venezuela and has family near the earthquake's epicenter. Anyone who can donate the use of a box truck is asked to contact Navarro at (954) 205-0700 or Marino at (772) 913-0805.

cards.headline: Fourth of July celebrations across Treasure Coast mark America's 250th birthday
cards.teaser: Communities across Palm Beach County and the Treasure Coast are hosting celebrations Saturday to mark America's 250th birthday, with events including fireworks, concerts, and time capsule openings.
cards.body:
Delray Beach's annual Fourth of July Celebration will begin at 5 p.m. on East Atlantic Avenue and A1A, drawing more than 20,000 people for a family-friendly tradition that has continued for over 50 years. The celebration includes a 1976 Bicentennial Time Capsule opening at 5 p.m. on the main stage at A1A, a 60-foot flag raising with the national anthem at 6 p.m. at Atlantic Avenue and Seabreeze Avenue, and live music starting at 6:30 p.m. Fireworks will launch at 9 p.m. All day activities beginning at 8 a.m. include a 4's on the 4th Volleyball Tournament at the south end of the municipal beach, a sand sculpting contest sponsored by Delray Beach Rotary and Kiwanis Clubs, snorkeling and scuba dive tours of the S.S. Inchulva "Delray Wreck" from 9 a.m. to 1 p.m., food trucks, vendors, arts and crafts, face painting, glitter tattoos, carnival games, photo booth, and toddler soft play.

Lake Worth Beach will host its Fourth of July Celebration at Bryant Park starting at noon with the Great American Raft Race hosted by the Neighborhood Association Presidents' Council. The city will celebrate with its first-ever drone show featuring 300 drones for 15 minutes at 8:45 p.m., best viewed from Bryant Park facing southwest. A concert by Sekond Nature starts at 7 p.m., followed by a skydiving performance by the All Veteran Group at 7:45 p.m., including a tandem jump by Vice Mayor Mimi May carrying a special American flag commemorating the nation's 250th anniversary. Concerts by Elton and the Jets, an Elton John tribute band, will perform at 8:30 and 9:30 p.m. Fireworks will launch at 9 p.m. with six minutes and 11,700 shots.

cards.headline: West Palm Beach woman raises funds for best friend's family after Venezuela earthquakes kill relatives
cards.teaser: Carla Alvarado of West Palm Beach launched a GoFundMe campaign to support her best friend's family in Venezuela after two devastating earthquakes killed multiple relatives and destroyed their homes.
cards.body:
Alessandra De La Correa spent six agonizing hours wondering if her parents were alive after two devastating earthquakes struck Venezuela's coastal city of La Guaira last week, collapsing buildings and killing family members. Her parents survived, but De La Correa lost her 17-year-old cousin Claudia, her grandmother, her uncle and his wife. Claudia, who had planned to study dentistry, was a volleyball player rehearsing a dance routine with classmates when the building collapsed. De La Correa's uncle, a former Navy member, searched through rubble in darkness and found Claudia dead beneath the debris. He stayed to help rescue her trapped best friend, who had been asking not to be left to die for around 13 hours, but the girl was later killed when another section of the structure collapsed during rescue efforts.

The earthquakes also destroyed De La Correa's parents' home and businesses. Her mother's children's clothing store was located inside a shopping mall that collapsed entirely, though her parents survived because they had closed early and were driving home when the quake struck. De La Correa's best friend since high school, Carla Alvarado, who now lives in West Palm Beach, launched a GoFundMe campaign to support the family. The campaign aims to raise $15,000 to help cover necessities like food, shelter and clothing as De La Correa's parents search the ruins of their apartment building for salvageable belongings.

cards.headline: Wellington Green's vacant Nordstrom could be converted into 620-unit apartment complex
cards.teaser: Bainbridge Companies has submitted plans to transform the vacant Nordstrom at the Mall at Wellington Green into a 620-unit apartment complex across 18 acres.
cards.body:
Bainbridge Companies has submitted plans to convert 18 acres of the vacant Nordstrom at the Mall at Wellington Green into a 620-unit multifamily apartment complex. If approved, the existing building would be demolished. Village Manager Jim Barnes said the development would include one-, two- and three-bedroom units along with three towers and a parking structure, as well as shared amenities. Barnes stated the project addresses a housing shortage not only in the county and state, but out of state as well.

Not all residents support the proposal. Richard Meyers, who has lived in Wellington for more than a decade, opposes adding more apartments to the area, noting there are already multiple apartment complexes around the mall. Other residents expressed concerns about traffic impacts. Gaby Martinez said the added density could strain local roads and create bottlenecks from daily commutes. However, Barnes suggested new development near the mall could benefit existing retailers. He noted that Macy's, Dillard's and JCPenney are high-performing stores, and said the Macy's at the Mall at Wellington Green is the highest-performing store in the state. No timeline or cost estimate has been announced, and the plans have not been approved.

hero.headline: North Palm Beach celebrates Fourth of July with fireworks and America 250 events at country club
hero.teaser: North Palm Beach Country Club and The Clubhouse will host a full day of Independence Day activities on July 4, including a pool party, live music and a 9 p.m. fireworks finale.
hero.body:
North Palm Beach will host a full day of Independence Day celebrations on July 4 at the North Palm Beach Country Club and The Clubhouse. The free community event combines family-friendly activities, live entertainment and fireworks to mark both the nation's birthday and America's 250th anniversary. According to event organizers, recognizing the milestone adds special significance to this year's annual holiday tradition in Palm Beach County.

The day begins at 11 a.m. with a community pool party at the country club pool area. Attendees can enjoy a water slide, DJ entertainment, games, activities, food and beverages, and a poolside satellite bar. Event organizers note that the pool deck and lawn areas will create a festive backdrop throughout the day. As the afternoon progresses, families can participate in lawn games and activities starting at 4:30 p.m., including cornhole, Connect 4, giant Jenga and face painting.

The Clubhouse will host a Fourth of July barbecue buffet beginning at 4:30 p.m., providing dinner options for guests. Live music from the band Solstice Reign is scheduled to begin around 6 p.m., adding entertainment to the evening festivities. Ashley Shipman, director of parks and recreation, highlighted that the golf course offers one of the best vantage points for viewing the fireworks display.

The celebration concludes with a fireworks finale at 9 p.m. The combination of activities, dining and entertainment makes the event accessible to visitors of all ages. With no admission fee and multiple entertainment options spread throughout the day, North Palm Beach's Fourth of July celebration provides a traditional way for residents and visitors to mark the holiday while also commemorating the country's 250-year milestone.

cards.headline: Loggerhead Marinelife Center in Juno Beach offers sea turtle nesting programs through September
cards.teaser: Loggerhead Marinelife Center in Juno Beach is offering a variety of educational and interactive programs during peak sea turtle nesting season this summer.
cards.body:
Loggerhead Marinelife Center in Juno Beach is offering educational and interactive programs through September during peak sea turtle nesting season. Guests can participate in guided Turtle Walks, the Hatchling Discovery Program, Hatchling Releases, Tidal Tots and Plastic Free July Community Action Day. The center's Turtle Walk program allows participants to observe the nesting process while learning about sea turtle biology, conservation and ongoing research efforts. Educational demonstrations may include the use of red-light headlamps, amber lighting, night scopes and research tag scanning equipment.

The programs are designed to give visitors an opportunity to learn more about sea turtle conservation along one of the world's busiest sea turtle nesting beaches. The center's education and research departments work together during nesting season to collect and analyze data related to nesting activity and hatchling success. Sea turtle nesting season in Florida typically runs from March through October. Conservation groups continue encouraging beachgoers to turn off beachfront lighting at night, properly dispose of trash and avoid disturbing nesting turtles or hatchlings. Registration information and program details are available through Loggerhead Marinelife Center.

hero.headline: Meta complies with Florida youth social media law while TikTok, Google face enforcement action
hero.teaser: Attorney General James Uthmeier said Meta has suspended hundreds of thousands of underage accounts and is complying with Florida's social media law, but TikTok and Google have stayed silent on their compliance plans.
hero.body:
Florida's landmark social media law took effect after a major legal victory in November when the 11th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals cleared the way for implementation. HB 3, which bans children under 14 from creating social media accounts and requires parental consent for users ages 14 and 15, passed the Legislature in March 2024 and was signed that same month by Governor Ron DeSantis. The law represented a signature priority for then-House Speaker Paul Renner, who argued that "a child in their brain development doesn't have the ability to know that they're being sucked into these addictive technologies."

Attorney General James Uthmeier moved swiftly to enforce the law after defeating Big Tech's legal challenge. He warned noncompliant platforms of $50,000-per-violation fines that could accumulate into billions of dollars. Meta responded by announcing compliance effective in early May, and Uthmeier confirmed that Meta has suspended hundreds of thousands of accounts belonging to underage users. By contrast, TikTok and Google, which owns YouTube and YouTube Kids, have remained silent about their compliance plans and have effectively ignored the law's requirements.

Uthmeier sued TikTok in June for violating HB 3 by allowing underage accounts to persist and failing to secure parental consent from older teens. "TikTok knowingly deceives parents and allows children to be exposed to harmful and inappropriate content in direct violation of Florida law," Uthmeier stated. He emphasized that "we have zero tolerance for companies that prioritize profit over children's safety." At a subsequent press conference, Uthmeier directed his message toward other holdouts, telling YouTube and other platforms: "You got to wake up. This is real and you can save lives."

Google's continued silence is particularly striking given YouTube's dominance in teens' online activities. Research from Pew found that roughly 90 percent of U.S. teenagers use YouTube, surpassing all other platforms, with about 75 percent using it daily. The exposure risks are well documented: 46 percent of parents with children ages 11 and younger who use YouTube reported their child had encountered inappropriate content on the platform. Even YouTube Kids, which is rated for ages 4 and up, has been found to serve children content on topics like gender ideology and systemic racism, according to congressional testimony. Whether Google, TikTok, Roblox, and other platforms will follow Meta's lead remains uncertain. If they do not comply, Uthmeier indicated that companies "will have to open up your checkbook."

cards.headline: DeSantis vetoes bill to raise sovereign immunity caps, ending bipartisan push for government liability reform
cards.teaser: Governor Ron DeSantis vetoed legislation that would have increased for the first time in 16 years the caps on damages payable to people harmed by government negligence, saying the increase would generate more unmeritorious lawsuits.
cards.body:
Gov. Ron DeSantis vetoed HB 145 on Monday, rejecting legislation that would have raised sovereign immunity caps for the first time in 16 years. The bill, which passed with overwhelming bipartisan support in March, would have increased damage caps from $200,000 per person and $300,000 per incident to $350,000 per person and $500,000 per incident. It would have also allowed local governments to voluntarily settle claims exceeding those caps without legislative approval. DeSantis said the increase would "generate more unmeritorious lawsuits" and opposed the measure on those grounds.

The legislation was sponsored by Sarasota Republican Rep. Fiona McFarland and Lake Mary Republican Sen. Jason Brodeur. McFarland framed the issue as one of equal protection under the law, arguing that claimants face prohibitive obstacles depending on whether the offender was a public or private entity. More than 240 lobbyists registered to speak about the bill, including representatives from counties, cities and their agencies facing budget shortfalls under a proposed property tax amendment on the November ballot. DeSantis defended his veto by noting that the Legislature clears roughly a third of the dozen claims bills it considers annually, arguing the current system works without fundamental changes.

cards.headline: Florida moves to designate CAIR, Muslim Brotherhood, Antifa as terrorist organizations under new state law
cards.teaser: Governor Ron DeSantis announced Wednesday that Florida will designate several groups as terrorist organizations under a new state law that took effect July 1, m.
cards.body:
Governor Ron DeSantis announced Wednesday that Florida will immediately use a new state law to designate several groups as terrorist organizations. At a Tampa press conference with FDLE Commissioner Mark Glass and Statewide Prosecutor Brad McVay, DeSantis said the state is preparing its first designations under HB 1471, which took effect July 1. The list includes the Muslim Brotherhood, the Council on American-Islamic Relations (CAIR), Antifa, cartel-linked groups including Tren de Aragua and Sinaloa-related organizations, and Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. HB 1471, formally titled "Systems of Law and Terrorist Organizations," authorizes Florida's Chief of Domestic Security to recommend terrorist designations that must be approved or rejected by the governor and Florida Cabinet by majority vote. Designated organizations face public-funding restrictions, possible corporate dissolution in certain circumstances, and penalties tied to material support.

DeSantis framed the announcement as strengthening a December executive order targeting CAIR and the Muslim Brotherhood that was temporarily blocked by a judge in March after civil rights groups sued, arguing it violated constitutional protections. DeSantis said the new law provides better legal footing. The consequences could affect state and local funding, colleges and universities, and Florida's K-12 school-choice scholarship program. Following the announcement, attorneys representing CAIR said they expect another court fight. While the designations are not final until the Cabinet approves them, DeSantis said officials may meet in an emergency session to approve them despite no regular Cabinet meeting scheduled in July.

cards.headline: Florida Chamber poll finds 64% of Floridians very proud to be American on 250th anniversary
cards.teaser: A statewide poll conducted by the Florida Chamber of Commerce shows most Floridians are proud to be Americans during the 250th anniversary of the signing of the Declaration of Independence, though responses fall along partisan lines.
cards.body:
A statewide poll conducted by the Florida Chamber of Commerce shows 64% of Floridians say they are "very proud" to be American as the nation marks the 250th anniversary of the Declaration of Independence. Another 12% say they are "somewhat proud," while 12% indicate they are not proud at all. Mark Wilson, President and CEO of the Florida Chamber of Commerce, said, "Two hundred and fifty years ago the Founding Fathers set America on a course that has shaped the world ever since. As America celebrates this milestone anniversary, the Florida Chamber celebrates and takes pride in our nation, in Florida's national leadership, and in the entrepreneurial spirit that defines America to this day."

The poll revealed significant partisan divisions on American pride. Some 89% of Republicans surveyed say they are very proud Americans, compared to 34% of Democrats and 58% of no-party voters. About 25% of Democrats say they're not proud at all of being American, while only 2% of Republicans and 12% of no-party voters say the same. Age also significantly affected responses, with 71% of Floridians over 60 saying they're very proud to be American versus 42% of those under 40. On American history generally, 74% of Florida voters say Americans should be proud of the nation's history, with 91% of Republicans and 51% of Democrats agreeing. The Florida Chamber survey included 604 likely voters between May 1 and May 9.

cards.headline: Saint Leo University and Town of St. Leo secure nearly $3 million in state budget for nursing, cybersecurity programs
cards.teaser: A trio of budget projects worth nearly $3 million survived Governor Ron DeSantis's veto pen, delivering funding for Saint Leo University's nursing and cybersecurity programs and stormwater infrastructure for the Town of St. Leo.
cards.body:
Saint Leo University and the Town of St. Leo secured nearly $3 million in state funding that survived Gov. Ron DeSantis' veto pen. The $117.6 billion budget signed this week allocated $1.2 million to expand the university's nursing program, $602,000 for its Cybersecurity and Cyberforensics Training and Education Center, and $995,000 for stormwater infrastructure supporting the Town of St. Leo's proposed town center. The nursing funding addresses a statewide priority, as Florida faces a projected shortage of nearly 60,000 nurses by 2035, according to the Florida Hospital Association. Saint Leo's nursing program has grown rapidly, jumping from 77 incoming pre-nursing students in Fall 2024 to 124 in Fall 2025, with enrollment expected to exceed 150 this Fall.

The nursing project will reconfigure existing campus space to add three classrooms, a nursing lab, faculty offices, simulation equipment and classroom technology upgrades. The cybersecurity investment will fund construction of a Security Operations Center and cyberforensics laboratory, providing hands-on training in digital defense, network monitoring and digital forensics, while supporting recruitment of additional faculty for undergraduate and graduate programs. Zephyrhills Republican Sen. Danny Burgess and Dade City Republican Rep. Randy Maggard sponsored the budget requests. The town's $995,000 will support stormwater improvements for the proposed St. Leo Town Center, a mixed-use development envisioned as a central gathering place featuring restaurants, retail, walking trails, a pavilion, botanical gardens and public gathering areas.

cards.headline: U.S. Sugar deploys autonomous tractors in largest commercial rollout in American sugar industry
cards.teaser: U.S. Sugar announced the largest commercial rollout of autonomous tractors in the American sugar industry, deploying five John Deere tractors retrofitted to operate around the clock without a driver in the cab near Clewiston.
cards.body:
U.S. Sugar has deployed four John Deere 8R Series tractors and one 9R Series machine in what the company calls the largest commercial commercial rollout of autonomous tractors in the American sugar industry. Each tractor has been retrofitted to operate around the clock without a driver in the cab, with a single technician monitoring several machines at once from a remote command center. The autonomous technology comes from Autonomous Solutions, Inc., a Utah-based company whose Vehicle Automation Kit is installed on the tractors' existing systems. The tractors were supplied by Everglades Equipment Group.

For workers like Harman Avalos, the transition is significant. After three years of driving tractors for up to ten hours a day, Avalos now monitors those same machines from an air-conditioned trailer with a laptop. Precision Agriculture Manager Scott Berden noted that farming today is far more high-tech than most people realize. The current fleet of five autonomous tractors is only the beginning. U.S. Sugar plans to eventually expand the technology across its entire 250,000-acre operation, an area stretching about 375 miles and nearly ten times the size of Miami. The feature appears in Florida Trend's July issue and online at FloridaTrend.com.

cards.headline: Arizona Senator Mark Kelly endorses two Florida Democrats challenging GOP House incumbents
cards.teaser: Arizona Senator Mark Kelly endorsed Bale Dalton's effort to unseat Representative Cory Mills and Darren McAuley's effort to defeat Representative Gus Bilirakis in their respective congressional races.
cards.body:
Arizona Democrat Mark Kelly, a retired Navy captain and former astronaut, endorsed two Florida Democrats challenging Republican House incumbents. Kelly announced his support during a social media event backing 10 Democrats with military backgrounds running for Congress. Bale Dalton is seeking to unseat GOP U.S. Rep. Cory Mills, a New Smyrna Republican in Florida's 7th Congressional District. Dalton, recently named to the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee's Red to Blue program, served 24 years in the Navy and Navy Reserve and previously worked as Chief of Staff for NASA. Kelly said Dalton knows the meaning of service and is running to put people over politics and deliver results for Florida families struggling to get by.

Darren McAuley is running in Florida's 12th Congressional District to challenge 20-year incumbent Gus Bilirakis, a Palm Harbor Republican. McAuley is a former Veterans Affairs physician and Florida's State Air Surgeon. Kelly said McAuley is a physician and veteran who has spent his life helping others, including fellow service members and veterans. Both candidates welcomed the endorsement. Dalton said he would keep working to lower the cost of living, while McAuley said it was an honor to have Kelly standing with him in the fight.

hero.headline: Martin County free clinic sees surge in patients after ACA subsidies expire, has capacity for more
hero.body:
Volunteers in Medicine in Martin County is treating more patients after enhanced subsidies through the Affordable Care Act expired at the start of 2026, leaving many people without health insurance. The clinic serves low-income families and provides free medical care with no strings attached.

Dr. Jordan Bromberg, medical director of Volunteers in Medicine, said more than 200,000 people in Florida did not renew their health insurance through the ACA this year. He estimates upwards of 500 people in Martin County lost access to health coverage. So far, about 20 patients have turned to the clinic after losing their ACA coverage. Rokaya McGarry is one of those patients. After the enhanced ACA subsidies expired, she could no longer afford health insurance. She fell very ill after losing her mother and began to see medical care as a luxury until it became a necessity. She called the clinic and was seen within a day.

Bromberg emphasized the importance of early medical screening. He said the expiration of the enhanced financial assistance program has left many people without any access to medical care. When health conditions are found early through screening, they can prevent serious outcomes. McGarry described her situation during that difficult time. "Panic set in because you know that the only way that you're going to be helped as far as health is to go to an Emergency," she said. After calling the clinic in her moment of desperation, she expressed deep gratitude for the care she received. "I can't even express how grateful I am to them because I don't know where I'd be," McGarry said.

To qualify for care at Volunteers in Medicine, individuals must earn under $39,990 per year, or under $82,500 for a family of four. Despite the influx of new patients, Bromberg said the clinic has room to serve more people from the community. "There are so many more out there that can come and see us," he said. "We have the capacity for more." The clinic continues to provide medical services at no cost to qualifying patients, making it an important resource for those who have lost insurance coverage and have limited financial means to pay for healthcare.

cards.headline: Jensen Beach teen Harper Aberman to represent Team USA at Sailing World Championship in France
cards.teaser: Harper Aberman, a Jensen Beach teenager, will represent Team USA at the Sailing World Championship in France starting Monday after training in Spain.
cards.body:
Harper Aberman started sailing at age four during a four-week summer camp in Pennsylvania that her grandparents enrolled her in. After initially attending for four weeks, she returned for eight weeks the following summer. When her family moved to Jensen Beach, Aberman joined the green fleet program at the US Sailing Center of Martin County, where her competitive sailing career took off. She has won countless tournaments, placed in several national competitions, and is considered one of the biggest names in the youth sailing circuit.

Aberman describes herself as an adrenaline junkie drawn to the sport's most challenging conditions, particularly windy weather. She received the email notifying her that she would represent Team USA during Spring Break, a moment she celebrated with her parents. Aberman has spent the past few weeks training in Spain ahead of the Sailing World Championship in France. Racing is set to begin Monday.

cards.headline: Martin County manufactured homeowners can apply for new state repair funding starting in August
cards.teaser: Martin County will open an online portal in August for manufactured homeowners to apply for emergency repairs and storm-hardening retrofits under a new state law that took effect Wednesday.
cards.body:
Senate Bill 594 took effect July 1st and opens up $167 million in state affordable housing funding to help mobile and manufactured home owners pay for emergency repairs and storm-hardening retrofits. The change follows an investigation that found nearly 700,000 mobile and manufactured homes in Florida, about two-thirds of the state's more than 1 million total, were built before today's federal safety standards, leaving them unable to withstand modern storms. The investigation began after an EF-3 tornado obliterated 138 homes in the Spanish Lakes Country Club Community of Fort Pierce, killing six residents.

Julie Stellatos with Martin County Human Services said an online portal will open in August. About 75 percent of the county's annual SHIP funding, typically $1 million to $1.5 million, could now help eligible mobile and manufactured homeowners. Applicants can fill out an online application or call the office to have one mailed. Stellatos said people were asking for help long before the law passed. The funding is first come, first served, so it is a matter of getting paperwork together as quickly as possible. Spanish Lakes resident Paula Richards received estimates costing $10,000 to $15,000 for repairs after the tornado.

cards.headline: Alligator Alcatraz immigration detention facility in Everglades closes after one year of controversy
cards.teaser: The controversial Alligator Alcatraz immigration detention facility in the Everglades closed in June, one year after Florida and the federal government opened it to house immigration detainees.
cards.body:
One year after its July 1, 2025 opening, Florida's Alligator Alcatraz immigration detention facility in the Everglades has closed following months of controversy. President Donald Trump and Gov. Ron DeSantis announced the facility's opening, describing it as a place to house dangerous migrants. The state used emergency powers to commandeer an old Miami-Dade County landing strip and built the facility in eight days using emergency funding and no-bid contracts through the Florida Division of Emergency Management. Trump said FEMA would cover costs, but a $608 million FEMA grant approved in October was stalled, leaving Florida taxpayers responsible. Total costs exceeded $1 billion according to most estimates. DeSantis said 21,000 detainees were deported through the facility.

The facility faced immediate legal and operational challenges. Using ICE data, investigators found approximately 70 percent of detainees had no criminal record, contradicting government claims. The American Civil Liberties Union sued over detainees' limited access to legal counsel, while Friends of the Everglades filed a separate lawsuit claiming construction violated the National Environmental Policy Act. A district court judge issued a preliminary injunction in August ordering dismantling of the facility, but an appeals court reversed the decision in September. ICE confirmed on June 16 that all detainees had been removed in preparation for hurricane season. Both lawsuits remain active.

cards.headline: West Palm Beach woman raises funds for best friend's family after Venezuela earthquakes
cards.teaser: Carla Alvarado of West Palm Beach launched a GoFundMe campaign to support her best friend's family after devastating earthquakes struck Venezuela's coastal city of La Guaira last week.
cards.body:
Alessandra De La Correa spent six agonizing hours wondering whether her parents were alive after two devastating earthquakes struck Venezuela's coastal city of La Guaira last week, collapsing buildings and killing members of her family. Her parents survived, but several relatives did not. De La Correa lost her 17-year-old cousin Claudia, her grandmother, her uncle and his wife. Claudia, a volleyball player, had been rehearsing a dance routine with classmates when the building collapsed. De La Correa's uncle, a former Navy member, found Claudia dead beneath the debris and stayed to help rescue her trapped best friend, but the girl was later killed when another section of the structure collapsed during rescue efforts after approximately 13 hours.

The earthquake destroyed De La Correa's parents' home and businesses. Her mother's children's clothing store had been located inside a shopping mall that collapsed entirely. Her parents survived only because they had closed the store early and were driving home when the earthquake struck. De La Correa's best friend since high school, Carla Alvarado, who now lives in West Palm Beach, launched a GoFundMe campaign to support De La Correa's relatives. The campaign aims to raise $15,000 and is quickly spreading.

cards.headline: Palm Beach County residents hit with thousands in retroactive sewer fees from Delray Beach
cards.teaser: Homeowners along Franwood Drive in unincorporated Palm Beach County received notices from Delray Beach demanding up to three years of retroactive sewer fees, with some bills totaling more than $4,000.
cards.body:
Several homeowners along Franwood Drive in an unincorporated Palm Beach County neighborhood received notices from the city of Delray Beach demanding back payments after a recent audit. The bills cover up to three years of charges, along with new monthly sewer fees going forward. Candace Etzler said at least a dozen homeowners in the neighborhood received similar notices. Etzler is being charged $3,139, while neighbor Ruth Stephens received a bill totaling $4,494.92. The situation dates back to 1998, when nearby development disrupted their septic systems and state law required them to connect to the closest municipal sewer system. The city completed an audit in April 2026, which triggered the retroactive billing.

City Commissioner Juli Casale responded with a statement defending the billing, saying that when a sewer connection is identified, the city's responsibility is to determine what costs were incurred and recover the applicable fees. County Commissioner Marci Woodward said she has been in touch with the county attorney, who will be looking into the legality of the back charges and monthly payments going forward. Some residents have already paid the fees or enrolled in payment plans, fearing disconnection of their service.

cards.headline: Stuart Bell named new University of Florida president after two-year search
cards.teaser: Stuart Bell was named the new University of Florida president, concluding a two-year search.
cards.body: Stuart Bell was named the new University of Florida president Wednesday, concluding a two-year search. The announcement marks the end of a lengthy selection process for the state's flagship university.

hero.headline: Atlantic High School to meet Vero Beach in August 28 football game
